events.title: Manasseh, a vassal of Assyria
events.text: Hezekiah's son Manasseh ruled Judah for many years as a vassal of Assyria. His name, 'Manasseh of Judah', is written on the inscriptions of Esarhaddon and of Ashurbanipal, among the western kings who brought them tribute. In the lowlands, towns Sennacherib had ruined began to live again.
events.why: The Bible paints Manasseh as the worst of Judah's kings, who rebuilt the high places and shed innocent blood. Chronicles adds a story, not in Kings, that he was taken in chains to Babylon and there repented. The inscriptions show a long, quiet vassalage.
claims: Manasseh of Judah named among Esarhaddon's and Ashurbanipal's western vassals.
Lowland towns destroyed in 701 BC were partly reoccupied under Manasseh.
He rebuilt the high places and shed innocent blood: 2 Kings 21.
Taken to Babylon, he repented: 2 Chronicles 33. Kings says nothing of this.

events.title: A blessing on silver
events.text: In a family tomb at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, archaeologists found two tiny silver scrolls, rolled up as amulets. Scratched into the silver is a blessing: 'The Lord bless you and keep you.' It is the oldest known text of a passage that still stands in the Hebrew Bible, the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.
events.why: The tomb belongs to the last generations before the city fell. The words were already being worn as a charm, close to the body, in Josiah's or Zedekiah's day.
claims: Two silver amulets from a tomb at Ketef Hinnom.
They carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, the oldest known text of this biblical passage.

events.title: Josiah and the book of the law
events.text: The Book of Kings says that in Josiah's eighteenth year a book of the law was found in the Temple. The king tore his clothes and began a reform: the high places were pulled down, worship was gathered to Jerusalem, and a great Passover was kept. At Arad, in the south, a small temple in the fortress was carefully taken apart and buried.
events.why: How much of the story of the lost book is memory, and how much is a later telling, is debated. Some link the buried shrine at Arad with Josiah; others date that burial earlier, to Hezekiah's time.
claims: The finding of the book and Josiah's reform: 2 Kings 22–23.
The shrine at Arad was dismantled and buried.
Whether the burial belongs to Josiah's reform, or earlier, is debated.
How much of the lost-book story is history is debated.

events.title: Nineveh falls, and Carchemish
events.text: In 612 BC the Babylonians and the Medes took Nineveh, the great Assyrian capital, and burned it. Pharaoh Neco marched north to help the last Assyrians. In 605 BC, at Carchemish on the Euphrates, Nebuchadnezzar broke the Egyptian army. A Babylonian chronicle records the battle. The west, including Judah, passed into Babylon's hand. The next year Ashkelon was taken and burned.
events.why: The Bible says Josiah went out to meet Neco at Megiddo and was killed. Neco's campaign is known from Egyptian and Greek writers; Josiah's death is told only in the Bible.
claims: Nineveh fell in 612 BC to the Babylonians and the Medes.
Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC.
Neco's march is known from Egyptian and Greek writers.

events.title: The first exile, 597 BC
events.text: A Babylonian chronicle says that in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year he encamped against 'the city of Judah', and on the second day of Adar he took the city and seized its king. He appointed a king of his own choosing and took a heavy tribute to Babylon. The Bible names the young king Jehoiachin, says he had ruled three months, and that the officers, the craftsmen and the king himself were taken east. Zedekiah, his uncle, was put on the throne.
events.why: This is one of the closest agreements between a biblical narrative and a cuneiform chronicle in the whole story. The book that bears Ezekiel's name says he was among those taken, and that he would prophesy by a canal in Babylonia.
claims: The Chronicle: capture of the city of Judah and its king, 2 Adar, year 7 (16 March 597 BC).
Jehoiachin, the craftsmen and the officers taken; Zedekiah made king: 2 Kings 24:12–17.

events.title: The Lachish letters
events.text: Lachish, rebuilt after Sennacherib's siege, was again Judah's strong town in the lowlands when Babylon came. In its gatehouse excavators found letters written in ink on broken pottery. One officer writes to his lord: 'we are watching for the fire signals of Lachish, according to the signs you gave, for we cannot see Azekah.'
events.why: The usual reading is that Azekah had already fallen, and that these are the last days of Judah's defence in the lowlands. The city itself, Level II, ended in a great fire in the same campaign that destroyed Jerusalem.
claims: The ostraca from the gate of Lachish Level II.
That Azekah had already fallen is the usual inference.
Level II was destroyed by fire in the Babylonian campaign.

events.title: Jerusalem burned, and the Temple
events.text: In 586 BC, or, as some scholars reckon, 587 BC, Jerusalem fell. In the City of David and on the western hill, archaeologists have found rooms blackened by a great fire, arrowheads of a Babylonian type, and a layer of ash. The Bible says that in the fifth month the house of the Lord was burned, and the king's house, and every great house, and the walls were pulled down. Of the Temple itself, no burnt stone has been found that we can point to and say: this was Solomon's house.
events.why: The destruction of the city is attested in the ground. The burning of the Temple is told in the Bible, and in a memory that never let it go. The exact year depends on how the kings' reigns are counted.
claims: The city was destroyed in a great fire at the end of the Iron Age.
The exact year, 586 or 587 BC, is disputed.
The Temple, the palaces and the walls were burned: 2 Kings 25:8–10.
No identified remains of the Temple itself from the fire.

events.title: Yaukin, king of Judah, at the emperor's table
events.text: In Babylon, unbaked clay tablets list rations of oil for 'Yaukin, king of the land of Judah' and for his five sons, years after Jerusalem had fallen. A king of Judah was still being fed at the emperor's table, in exile. Other tablets, from a town in the Babylonian countryside called Al-Yahudu, 'the city of Judah', name Judean families farming and paying taxes a generation on.
events.why: The Bible gives more than one number for those taken to Babylon, and the numbers do not agree. The tablets show a real community in exile, and a king who had lost his city but not his title. Over those who remained, the Bible says, the Babylonians appointed Gedaliah at Mizpah. Archaeology finds life going on in Benjamin; the land was not empty.
claims: The ration tablets name Ya'u-kīnu, king of the land of Judah, and his sons.
Judean families at Āl-Yāḫūdu in rural Babylonia.
The Bible's numbers for the exiles do not agree: 2 Kings 24 and Jeremiah 52.
Life continued in Benjamin under Babylonian rule.

steps.text: The story so far.
In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
claims: In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
steps.display: In 1207 BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.

steps.text: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.
claims: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.

steps.text: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.
claims: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.

steps.text: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.
claims: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.

steps.text: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.
claims: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.

steps.text: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about nine thirty BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
claims: How large their kingdom was is debated.
By about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
steps.display: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.

steps.text: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.
claims: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.

steps.text: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.
claims: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.

steps.text: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich, and the prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.
claims: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich.
The prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.

steps.text: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
claims: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
steps.display: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser III takes Damascus and Galilee, and in 722 BC Samaria falls.

steps.text: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.
claims: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.

steps.text: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.
claims: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.

steps.text: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings. Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.
claims: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings.
Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.

steps.text: Sennacherib is later killed by his own son. The city has been spared.
